entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Marxism–Leninism was the official political ideology of the Soviet Union and the countries of the Eastern Bloc, shaping the course of modern history. Born in the early 20th century, its influence spread across the globe, particularly in the aftermath of the Russian Revolution of 1917. Lenin's ideas, initially an offshoot of Marxist thought, evolved into a distinct philosophical and political framework. Through its adoption by socialist and communist movements worldwide, Marxism–Leninism left a lasting impact on modern politics, economy, and society.


    The core of Marxism–Leninism lies in the concept of dialectical materialism, which posits that societal development is the result of class struggle between the bourgeoisie and proletariat. Lenin's adaptation of this theory led to the establishment of the Soviet Union, with a centrally planned economy and a one-party system. This system, in turn, had far-reaching consequences for international relations, as the Soviet Union became a superpower in the 20th century.


    The legacy of Marxism–Leninism can be seen in the continued influence of its ideas on socialist and communist movements globally, as well as in the resurgence of interest in Marxist thought in recent years. Furthermore, its impact on the development of modern capitalism and the rise of the United States as a global superpower cannot be overstated. The ideology's emphasis on class struggle and the role of the state in economic development also continues to shape contemporary debates on economic inequality and the role of government in the economy.


    A stark reminder of Marxism–Leninism's enduring legacy can be seen in the ongoing debates over the nature of socialism, communism, and the role of the state in modern society, as well as in the continued relevance of its ideas on class struggle and economic development.
